q: Suggest why breathing through the nose is better for the lungs than breathing through the mouth.

pts.a: The air is filtered, warmed and moistened in the nose, but not in the mouth
accept: the nose cleans the air
the air is warmed
the nose traps dust and germs

q: State the function of the mucus that lines the trachea.

traps particles

dust sticks to it

right: It traps dust and germs in the air breathed in
wrong: It keeps the trachea open so it does not collapse
It sweeps dust up to the throat
It lubricates food on its way to the stomach
why: Mucus is sticky: dust and microbes in the air breathed in get caught in it before they can reach the alveoli. The cilia then move it away.

q: State the function of the cilia that line the trachea and bronchi.

pts.a: They sweep (beat) the mucus and trapped dust up to the throat, away from the lungs

beat to push mucus upwards

right: They sweep the mucus and trapped dust up, away from the lungs, to the throat
wrong: They sweep dust down into the lungs
They trap dust in a sticky layer
They carry out gas exchange with the capillaries
why: Cilia are tiny hairs on the lining cells. They beat to move mucus, with the dust and germs stuck in it, up to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed up.

q: Smoke damages the cilia in the airways. Suggest why smokers often cough.

pts.a: Mucus is not swept away, so it builds up in the airways and has to be coughed up
accept: mucus builds up in the lungs
mucus collects in the airways
the mucus stays in the bronchi
the mucus is not removed
to get rid of the mucus

right: Mucus is not swept away, so it builds up and must be coughed up
wrong: The cilia beat faster and push the smoke into the lungs

why: With damaged cilia, the mucus and the dirt and germs trapped in it are no longer swept up out of the airways. The mucus builds up, and coughing is the only way to clear it.

q: State the function of the bronchioles.

pts.a: Carry air to (and from) the alveoli
accept: take air into the air sacs
carry air from the bronchi to the alveoli
bring air to the alveoli for gas exchange

why: The bronchioles are the many fine branches of each bronchus. They carry air deep into the lung, right to the alveoli, where gas exchange takes place.

q: The pharynx is part of both the breathing system and the digestive system. Explain why.

pts.a: Both air and food pass through it

wrong: It makes sounds when air passes over it

why: The pharynx (throat) is a shared passage: air goes through it on its way to the larynx, and food goes through it on its way to the oesophagus.

q: What is meant by a concentration gradient?

pts.a: A difference in the concentration of a substance between two regions
accept: the difference in concentration between two areas
a concentration difference between two places

right: A difference in concentration between two regions
wrong: The movement of molecules from high to low concentration
The total amount of a substance dissolved in a solution
The speed at which a gas diffuses across a membrane
why: A concentration gradient is a difference in concentration between two places. Diffusion is movement down that gradient, so the steeper the gradient, the faster the diffusion.

q: Explain how breathing helps to keep the concentration gradient of oxygen steep at the alveolus.

pts.a: Each breath brings fresh air, high in oxygen, into the alveoli, replacing the used air
accept: it keeps bringing in fresh air
new air keeps arriving
it replaces the air in the alveoli
it keeps the oxygen concentration in the alveoli high
it renews the air

right: It keeps bringing fresh air, high in oxygen, into the alveoli
wrong: Breathing pumps oxygen across the alveolus wall into the blood
It keeps the oxygen level in the blood high
It makes the walls of the alveoli thinner
why: Each breath replaces used air in the alveoli with fresh air, so the oxygen concentration there stays higher than in the blood, and oxygen keeps diffusing in.

q: Explain how the flow of blood past the alveolus helps to keep the concentration gradient of oxygen steep.

pts.a: Moving blood carries the oxygen away, so the blood arriving at the alveolus is always low in oxygen
accept: the blood carries the oxygen away
oxygen is taken away to the body
new blood low in oxygen keeps arriving
deoxygenated blood keeps arriving from the pulmonary artery
the oxygen is removed by the blood

right: It carries the oxygen away, so arriving blood is always low in oxygen
wrong: Blood flows slowly so oxygen has more time to diffuse
Haemoglobin releases oxygen into the alveolus
Blood flows out of the capillaries into the alveolus
why: Blood keeps carrying newly absorbed oxygen away to the body, so the blood in the capillary always has less oxygen than the air in the alveolus.

the blood arriving is rich in CO2

pts.a: Breathing out removes the carbon dioxide from the alveolus

the air in the alveoli is kept low in CO2

why: Respiring cells keep adding carbon dioxide to the blood that comes to the lungs, while breathing out keeps the level in the alveolus low, so it keeps diffusing out of the blood.

q: Suggest why gas exchange in the lungs slows down if breathing stops.

pts.a: The air in the alveoli is not renewed, so the concentration gradients become less steep (oxygen is used up and carbon dioxide builds up in the alveoli)
accept: the concentration gradient gets smaller
no fresh air reaches the alveoli
carbon dioxide builds up in the alveoli
the oxygen in the alveoli gets used up
the difference in concentration falls

right: No fresh air arrives, so the concentration gradients become less steep
wrong: The alveoli collapse and lose their large surface area
The walls of the alveoli become thicker
Oxygen can only diffuse while the diaphragm is moving
why: Without breathing, the oxygen in the alveoli is used up and carbon dioxide builds up, so the difference in concentration between air and blood shrinks and diffusion slows.

why: The medulla oblongata is the brain's breathing centre. It sends impulses along nerves to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, so they contract faster and more strongly.

q: Explain how the extra carbon dioxide made during exercise leads to faster breathing.

pts.a: It makes the blood more acidic (its pH falls)

wrong: It takes in more oxygen, which neutralises the acid

why: Breathing faster and deeper exhales the extra carbon dioxide, so less acid forms in the blood and its pH rises back towards normal.

accept: CO2 levels in the blood rise
the blood becomes more acidic
the pH of the blood falls
carbon dioxide builds up and must be removed
the brain detects high carbon dioxide

right: Carbon dioxide has built up in the blood, making it more acidic
wrong: The level of oxygen in the blood has fallen, and the brain detects this

why: While the breath is held, carbon dioxide from respiration builds up and the blood's pH falls. The medulla oblongata detects this and drives fast, deep breaths to remove it.
